event: I am responsible for an important release next week.
rawInterpretation: Something will go wrong and everyone will blame me.
alternateRealityChecks: Large releases involve multiple safeguards and reviewers.
Potential issues can be addressed through preparation and monitoring.
Responsibility is usually shared across the team.
The worst-case scenario is only one possible outcome.
revisedInterpretation: There are risks, but many controls exist to reduce them.
chosenBehaviour: Focus on release preparation and mitigation plans.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The release completed successfully with only minor issues.

event: My work will be reviewed by senior leadership.
rawInterpretation: They will find major flaws that I missed.
alternateRealityChecks: Leadership reviews are often intended to provide guidance.
Senior stakeholders understand that no work is perfect.
Feedback does not necessarily imply failure.
There is no evidence that major flaws exist.
revisedInterpretation: The review may provide useful feedback rather than expose failure.
chosenBehaviour: Prepare thoroughly and remain open to feedback.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Leadership provided constructive suggestions and supported the proposal.

event: I made a small mistake in a status report.
rawInterpretation: People will lose confidence in me.
alternateRealityChecks: Everyone makes occasional mistakes.
A single error rarely defines professional reputation.
Correcting mistakes often matters more than avoiding them entirely.
There is no evidence people have lost trust.
revisedInterpretation: The mistake is unlikely to have a major impact on how I am perceived.
chosenBehaviour: Correct the issue and move forward.

event: I am starting a project involving technology I have never used before.
rawInterpretation: I am not capable enough for this project.
alternateRealityChecks: Learning new technologies is a normal part of growth.
Lack of experience does not mean lack of capability.
Support and learning resources are available.
Many experts were once beginners.
revisedInterpretation: This is a learning challenge rather than evidence of incompetence.
chosenBehaviour: Create a learning plan and seek help when needed.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Initial learning progressed faster than expected.

event: My code received several review comments.
alternateRealityChecks: Code reviews are designed to improve quality.
Experienced engineers also receive comments.
Comments focus on code, not personal worth.
Collaboration often produces better outcomes.
revisedInterpretation: The feedback is part of the engineering process.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The code was approved and merged.

event: I have been asked to lead a workshop for the first time.
rawInterpretation: People will realise I do not know enough.
alternateRealityChecks: You were likely selected because others believe you can contribute.
Facilitators do not need to know everything.
Workshops are collaborative by nature.
Uncertainty does not mean lack of competence.
revisedInterpretation: I can facilitate effectively even if I do not have all the answers.
chosenBehaviour: Prepare the agenda and focus on facilitating discussion.

event: The project is taking longer than originally estimated.
rawInterpretation: I am failing as a project lead.
alternateRealityChecks: Project delays often have multiple contributing factors.
Complex projects frequently require adjustment.
One challenge does not define leadership ability.
Managing uncertainty is part of project work.
revisedInterpretation: The delay is a project issue, not necessarily a personal failure.

event: A colleague completed a similar task much faster than I did.
rawInterpretation: I am falling behind everyone else.
alternateRealityChecks: People have different levels of experience and context.
Speed is not the only measure of value.
Quality and long-term impact also matter.
One comparison does not define overall capability.
revisedInterpretation: Their speed does not determine my worth as a professional.
chosenBehaviour: Focus on personal improvement rather than comparison.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The completed work received positive feedback from stakeholders.

event: An important decision depends on my recommendation.
rawInterpretation: If I choose incorrectly, my reputation will be damaged.
alternateRealityChecks: Decisions are made using available information, not hindsight.
Reasonable decisions can still have imperfect outcomes.
People are generally evaluated on process, not just outcomes.
Mistakes are part of learning and leadership.
revisedInterpretation: My responsibility is to make the best decision possible with current information.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The decision was accepted and supported by the team.

event: I received little feedback after completing a major task.
rawInterpretation: The work must not have been very good.
alternateRealityChecks: People often provide feedback only when changes are required.
Silence does not automatically imply dissatisfaction.
Stakeholders may be satisfied and focused on other priorities.
The absence of feedback is ambiguous.
revisedInterpretation: There is not enough information to draw conclusions about quality.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Stakeholders expressed appreciation for the work.

event: I have received similar feedback about communication gaps from multiple stakeholders over the last few months.
rawInterpretation: I am bad at communication and will never improve.
alternateRealityChecks: Receiving repeated feedback may indicate a genuine area for development.
A skill gap does not mean a permanent limitation.
Many communication skills can be learned and improved with deliberate practice.
The evidence supports improvement being needed, but not the belief that improvement is impossible.
revisedInterpretation: There appears to be a communication issue worth addressing, but it does not define my overall capability.
chosenBehaviour: Create an improvement plan and seek targeted feedback.
outcomeOneWeekLater: A manager suggested specific techniques and offered coaching opportunities.

event: I was asked a technical question during a meeting and could not answer it.
rawInterpretation: Everyone now thinks I am unqualified.
alternateRealityChecks: No one can know every answer in a complex domain.
Professionals regularly defer answers and follow up later.
One unanswered question is not sufficient evidence of incompetence.
The audience may have focused on the discussion rather than the missing answer.
revisedInterpretation: Not knowing one answer does not determine how others evaluate my expertise.
chosenBehaviour: Research the answer and follow up.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The follow-up answer was appreciated by the group.

event: My project has several unresolved risks and leadership keeps asking about them.
rawInterpretation: Leadership has lost confidence in me.
alternateRealityChecks: Projects with significant risks naturally receive more attention.
Leadership may be concerned about project outcomes rather than your competence.
The questions could indicate responsible governance.
However, addressing the risks promptly is important.
revisedInterpretation: Leadership is appropriately focused on project risks, and I should concentrate on managing them effectively.
chosenBehaviour: Strengthen mitigation plans and communicate transparently.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Leadership expressed appreciation for improved risk visibility.

event: A colleague pointed out an issue in my design that I had overlooked.
rawInterpretation: I am careless and should not be trusted with important work.
alternateRealityChecks: Design reviews exist because individuals naturally miss things.
Finding issues early improves outcomes.
One oversight does not justify a broad negative label.
The process worked as intended by identifying the issue before implementation.
revisedInterpretation: I missed something important, but that does not make me careless overall.
chosenBehaviour: Understand why the oversight occurred and improve review practices.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The design was updated and approved.

event: My manager said my recent performance has been below expectations and discussed a development plan.
alternateRealityChecks: The feedback indicates a real concern that should be taken seriously.
A development plan usually exists to support improvement rather than guarantee failure.
Performance can change significantly with focused effort and support.
The evidence supports improvement being necessary, but not the conclusion that your career is over.
revisedInterpretation: There is a legitimate performance concern that requires action, but improvement remains possible.
chosenBehaviour: Engage actively with the development plan and seek regular feedback.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Concrete improvement goals were established and support resources were provided.
